corpus_gaps: No rate Order made under section 3 of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 is in the corpus. Section 3 charges duty only 'at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette', so the rupee amount of duty on a lease and on a mortgage bond cannot be computed from the corpus. Q02 and Q03 both turn on that missing subsidiary legislation.
No exemption Order made under section 5 of Act No. 12 of 2006 is in the corpus, so any threshold or exemption applicable to a lease or a mortgage bond in April 2023 cannot be checked.

No statute in the corpus divides a deed of lease into parts or states what each part must contain. The conventional structure (introduction and parties, recitals, testatum, habendum, reddendum, covenants, testimonium) comes from conveyancing practice and the Roman-Dutch law of letting and hiring, neither of which is in the corpus. The Notaries Ordinance supplies only scattered content requirements.

The Schedules to the Notaries Ordinance (including Form E, the statutory attestation form referred to in section 31 rule (21), and Forms F and F1) are not extracted as corpus sections; only sections 1 to 43 are present.

Corpus texts are consolidated to 2024. The bodies of Notaries Ordinance section 31 and Prevention of Frauds Ordinance section 2 include changes made by the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 6 of 2024 and the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act, No. 4 of 2024, both later than the April 2023 matter date. Excerpts were taken from passages already in force in April 2023, but the surrounding text of those two sections is not the April 2023 text.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
provisions.why_relevant: A lease of the shop for a period exceeding one month creates an interest affecting immovable property and so falls inside section 2: it has no force in law unless reduced to writing, signed by the executants and the witnesses before a licensed notary and attested by him. This is why the transaction must take the form of a notarial deed at all, and it fixes the frame within which the parts of the deed are drafted.
provisions.temporal_note: The quoted opening words predate both the 2022 and the 2024 amendments and were in force in April 2023. The renumbering into subsection (1) and the new subsection (2) come from Act No. 4 of 2024, after the matter date; the subsection label here reflects the consolidated corpus text, not the April 2023 layout.

provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the physical form in which the drafted lease must be produced: original, duplicate and protocol. It bears on how the document as a whole is described, though it says nothing about the internal parts.
provisions.temporal_note: No amendment event recorded; in force from 1840 and unchanged at April 2023.

The question excludes the schedule, so this is context for the operative part rather than the answer itself.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: (18) He shall correctly insert in letters in every deed or instrument executed before him the day, month, and year on which and the place where the same is executed, and shall sign the same.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The question asks for the parts of a deed of lease and the contents of each. No provision in the corpus divides a deed into parts or says what a recital, habendum, reddendum or covenant clause must contain. That structure comes from the Roman-Dutch law of letting and hiring and from settled conveyancing precedent, neither of which is statutory. The corpus supplies only fragments of the content: that the instrument must be notarially executed and in triplicate, that the date and place must be inserted in letters, that the property description must appear in the deed or an annexed schedule, and that the true consideration must be set out. A complete answer needs the non-statutory drafting doctrine as well.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a lease of the shop premises at a monthly rent must be executed as a notarial deed at all, and in what physical form.

What the conventional parts of a deed of lease are (introduction and parties, recitals, operative or granting part, habendum fixing the term, reddendum fixing the rent, covenants and conditions, testimonium) and what each must contain.
Which of those contents are imposed by statute on the notary drafting the lease, and which rest on conveyancing practice only.

questions.hop_count_basis: Two steps on the statutory side: the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance requirement of notarial execution for a lease exceeding one month, then the Notaries Ordinance rules that fix particular contents of such a deed. gold_answer_draft.issue: What are the constituent parts of the notarial deed of lease of the shop at Assessment No. 12, Old Kottawa Road, Depanama, and what must each part contain, leaving aside the attestation and the schedule?
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month is within Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, so it has no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by every executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licensed notary and attested by him; by s.16 of the same Ordinance it must be executed in triplicate. The Notaries Ordinance prescribes some of what the instrument must contain. Section 31 rule (18) requires the notary to insert in letters the day, month and year on which and the place where the deed is executed. Section 31 rule (17)(a) requires an accurate and clear description of the property, showing its boundaries, extent and situation, either in the deed or in a schedule annexed to it. Section 38(1) requires the notary to ascertain the true and full consideration and to set it forth in the deed, which for a lease means the rent actually agreed. Section 31 rule (6) forbids attestation unless the notary has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided. Beyond these fragments the corpus contains no provision that divides a deed of lease into parts or fixes the content of any part; the conventional structure of introduction and parties, recitals, operative or granting words, habendum, reddendum, covenants and conditions, and testimonium rests on the Roman-Dutch law of letting and hiring and on conveyancing precedent, which are outside the corpus.
gold_answer_draft.application: On the enriched facts the lease runs for five years from 1 June 2023, so it is well outside the one-month exception and must be a notarial deed executed in triplicate. The introductory part would carry the date 20 May 2023 and the place, Maharagama, written in letters as s.31 rule (18) requires, together with the full names, addresses and descriptions of Shantha Silva as lessor and Asela Pathirana as lessee. The recitals would set out the lessor's title on Deed of Transfer No. 4127 and his agreement to lease. The operative part would demise the premises more fully described in the schedule, the description itself satisfying s.31 rule (17)(a). The habendum would fix the five-year term from 1 June 2023 and the reddendum the rent of Rs.50,000 a month payable in advance, which is the true consideration the notary must set out under s.38(1). The covenant part would carry the deposit, the rates and utilities obligation, the covenant against sub-letting and the right of re-entry, and the testimonium would recite execution by the parties. What the corpus cannot supply is authority for that division into parts, or for the required contents of the recitals, habendum, reddendum, covenants and testimonium as such.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The question can be answered only in part on statutory authority. The requirement of notarial execution in triplicate, the date and place in letters, the property description and the statement of the true rent are supported by the corpus. The rest of the answer, which is the substance of what the examiner asks for, depends on non-statutory conveyancing doctrine that is not in the corpus, so this question is reserved rather than proposed as gold.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month has no force in law unless it is in writing, signed by the executants and the witnesses before a licensed notary and attested by him.
Such a deed must be executed, acknowledged or attested in triplicate.
The notary must insert in letters the day, month and year on which and the place where the deed is executed.
The deed must embody, in itself or in an annexed schedule, an accurate and clear description of the property showing its boundaries, extent and situation.
The notary must ascertain the true and full consideration and set it forth in the deed, which for this lease is the agreed rent.
Because the agreed term is five years from 1 June 2023, the lease falls outside the exception for a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month and must be a notarial deed.
The introductory part would state 20 May 2023 and Maharagama in letters, together with the names and descriptions of the lessor and the lessee.
The reddendum would state the rent of Rs.50,000 a month payable in advance as the true consideration for the demise.

The division of the lease into introduction, recitals, operative part, habendum, reddendum, covenants and testimonium, and the contents required of each of those parts, cannot be supported from any provision in the corpus.

Statutory provisions cover only fragments of the content, so a statute-only gold answer would be incomplete and misleading.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: Stamp duty is wholly a creature of statute. Whether the lease is chargeable, who pays and when are all answered by the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006, and no judicial authority or common law doctrine is needed. The rupee figure depends on a Ministerial Order made under section 3 of that Act, which is subsidiary legislation rather than case law, so the authority requirement stays statutory even though that Order is missing from the corpus.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is payable on the lease agreement between Shantha Silva and Asela Pathirana, and by whom?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 s.3(1) charges stamp duty at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka. Section 4(i) makes a lease or hire of any property a specified instrument. Section 6(c) makes the duty on a lease payable by the lessee, otherwise than where there is an agreement to the contrary. Section 8(1) requires the duty to be paid by affixing adhesive stamps of the required value prior to or at the time of execution, and s.8(2) allows the duty on an instrument relating to a lease of immovable property to be paid to a prescribed bank, which issues a certificate to be affixed to the instrument. Section 13 leaves the imposition and exemption provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 without operation so far as inconsistent, save for transfers of immovable property, motor vehicle transfers and documents filed in court, none of which covers a lease. Section 5 leaves exemptions to be specified by Order in the Gazette. The Act itself fixes no rate.
gold_answer_draft.application: The instrument is a lease of the shop premises, so it is a specified instrument under s.4(i), and it is to be executed in Sri Lanka on 20 May 2023, so it falls within s.3(1)(a). The rent reserved for the five-year term is Rs.3,000,000 with no premium or other capital payment, so that is the consideration by reference to which duty would be computed. There being no agreement to the contrary, s.6(c) places the duty on the lessee, Asela Pathirana. Payment must be made by adhesive stamps before or at execution under s.8(1), or to a prescribed bank under s.8(2), and the notary may not attest the deed until he has an assurance under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6) that the duty is provided. The 1982 Act supplies no alternative rate for a lease, because s.13 of the 2006 Act displaces it. The rate itself is fixed only by an Order made by the Minister under s.3, and no such Order is in the corpus, so the rupee amount cannot be computed here.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The lease agreement is chargeable with stamp duty as a specified instrument, and the duty falls on the lessee, Asela Pathirana, to be paid before or at execution. The amount cannot be stated: the rate is set by a Gazette Order under s.3 of the 2006 Act which is not in the corpus, and the exemption Orders under s.5 are likewise absent, so the question is blocked for missing authority rather than answered with a figure.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka at such rate as the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette.
A lease or hire of any property is a specified instrument.
In the case of a lease the duty is payable by the lessee unless the parties have agreed otherwise.
The duty must be paid by affixing adhesive stamps of the required value before or at execution, or, on a lease of immovable property, to a prescribed bank which certifies payment.

The Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 supplies no rate for this lease, because its imposition provisions have no operation so far as inconsistent with the 2006 Act and the preserved exceptions do not cover a lease.
The lease of the shop premises, to be executed in Sri Lanka on 20 May 2023, is a specified instrument within the charge.
The consideration by reference to which duty would be computed is the rent of Rs.3,000,000 reserved for the five-year term, there being no premium or other capital payment.
There being no agreement to the contrary, the duty falls on the lessee, Asela Pathirana.
The rupee amount of duty cannot be calculated from the corpus, because the rate is fixed only by a Ministerial Order under section 3 that is not in the corpus.

added_facts.fact: The loan of Rs.4,000,000 is advanced in a single sum, the bond secures that fixed principal with interest, and no further or fluctuating advances are contemplated.
added_facts.reason: The charge on a bond or mortgage applies only where it is for a definite and certain sum of money. A facility for fluctuating advances would not plainly meet that condition.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the bond secured an overdraft or an unspecified running account, the sum would not be definite and certain and the instrument might fall outside paragraph (g) of the specified instruments.

added_facts.counterfactual_effect: A prior registered mortgage would leave the bank with a secondary security but would not alter the chargeability of the bond itself.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What stamp duty is payable on a mortgage bond by which Shantha Silva mortgages the shop premises to secure a loan of Rs.4,000,000, and who must pay it?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 s.3(1) charges duty at such rate as the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka. Section 4(g) makes a bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money and affecting any property a specified instrument. Section 6 places the duty, otherwise than where there is an agreement to the contrary, on the person drawing, making or executing the instrument in all cases for which no special rule is given, and no special rule is given for a mortgage. Section 8(1) requires payment by adhesive stamps prior to or at execution, and s.8(2) permits duty on an instrument relating to a mortgage of immovable property to be paid to a prescribed bank against a certificate affixed to the instrument. Section 13 leaves the 1982 Act without operation so far as inconsistent, save for transfers of immovable property, motor vehicle transfers and court documents, none of which covers a mortgage bond. Section 5 leaves exemptions to Gazette Order. The Act fixes no rate for a mortgage.
gold_answer_draft.application: The bond secures a single advance of Rs.4,000,000 with interest and contemplates no fluctuating advances, so it is a bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum of money, and it affects the shop premises, so it falls squarely within s.4(g). It is to be executed in Sri Lanka on 15 June 2023, so s.3(1)(a) applies. Shantha Silva alone executes it as mortgagor and there is no agreement to the contrary, so the duty falls on him under s.6. Payment must be made before or at execution under s.8(1), or to a prescribed bank under s.8(2), and the notary may not attest until he has an assurance under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6) that the duty is provided. The amount, however, depends on the rate the Minister has fixed for a mortgage by Order under s.3, and no such Order is in the corpus. The 1982 Act cannot serve as a substitute source of rate, because s.13 of the 2006 Act removes its operation for this instrument.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The mortgage bond is chargeable with stamp duty as a specified instrument, and the duty falls on Shantha Silva as the executant, payable before or at execution. The value of the duty on the Rs.4,000,000 bond cannot be stated from the corpus, because the rate Order made under s.3 of the 2006 Act and any exemption Order under s.5 are both absent, so this question is blocked for missing authority.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka at the rate the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette.
A bond or mortgage for any definite and certain sum of money and affecting any property is a specified instrument.
Where no special incidence rule is given, and absent an agreement to the contrary, the duty is payable by the person drawing, making or executing the instrument.
Duty on an instrument relating to a mortgage of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at execution, and otherwise must be met by adhesive stamps before or at execution.
The bond, securing a single advance of Rs.4,000,000 over the shop premises, is a bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum affecting property and so is within the charge.
The duty falls on Shantha Silva as the executant of the bond, there being no agreement to the contrary.

The Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 cannot supply the rate, because its imposition provisions have no operation so far as inconsistent with the 2006 Act and a mortgage bond is not within the preserved exceptions.
The value of the duty on the Rs.4,000,000 mortgage bond cannot be stated from the corpus, because the rate is fixed only by a Ministerial Order under section 3 that is not in the corpus.

questions.block_reason: The rate of stamp duty on a mortgage bond is fixed by Ministerial Order under section 3 of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006, and no such Order is in the corpus. The Act itself gives only the charge, the classification and the incidence, so the rupee value asked for cannot be produced without inventing a rate.
